purpose: Loxapine is used to treat schizophrenia, a condition that can cause hallucinations, delusions, and confused thinking. One inhaled form (Adasuve) is used in hospital settings to quickly calm agitation in people with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. It helps you think more clearly and feel more in control of your thoughts and behavior.
how_it_works: Loxapine works by blocking certain chemical messengers in your brain, mainly dopamine and serotonin, that can become overactive and cause symptoms like hallucinations or agitation. By calming down these overactive signals, your brain can function in a more balanced way. Think of it like turning down the volume on brain activity that has gotten too loud.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, stiff muscles or tremors, restlessness or feeling like you need to keep moving, and weight gain. Some people also feel lightheaded when standing up quickly.
warnings: Loxapine can cause a serious movement disorder called tardive dyskinesia with long-term use, which may be permanent. It may also lower the seizure threshold, so tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures. The inhaled form (Adasuve) can cause sudden bronchospasm (airway tightening), so it is only given in a hospital setting. Elderly patients with dementia who take antipsychotics have a higher risk of stroke or death — this medication is not approved for that use. Do not drink alcohol while taking this medication, and always rise slowly from sitting or lying down to avoid falls.
typical_dosing: For schizophrenia taken by mouth, the usual starting dose is 10 mg taken twice a day, and your doctor may gradually increase it up to 100 mg per day depending on how you respond. Most people end up on a maintenance dose between 60 and 100 mg per day divided into 2 to 4 doses. The inhaled form used in hospitals is a single 10 mg dose given one time for acute agitation. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
